output.methodChoice: EDF sequence; collected X11 and X5 (2 items, limit reached)

answers.answer_note: RD yield fell 39.0→31.5 but EA (legacy, no portal) fell almost as much, 45.2→37.8, so the portal delay cannot be separated from the common cause; RD-specific excess is small.
Yield fell most in tiers whose award was cut (Dean's 45.2→31.9, Merit 44.9→32.3); Presidential tier with unchanged award was flat (36.6→36.2); both rounds fell similarly.
Applications rose 9,850→10,240, admits rose 5,120→5,270, admitted GPA rose 3.61→3.63.
Only a counsellor complaint and a team claim that files were complete; no record of lost documents was collected.
Drop is concentrated in merit-discounted tiers; the no-merit tier and Presidential tier barely moved, so it is not a general demand softening.
Early action fell by a similar amount with no portal involvement, so the RD slowdown does not explain the drop; association at most.
Award cut is temporally prior, mechanism is direct, tier pattern with an unchanged comparison group rules out general softening.
Freeze and slower merit-eligible RD decisions (38 vs 16 days) are consistent, but only interview evidence; X9 staffing records not collected.
Admits and applications rose, so a smaller pool did not reduce enrolment.
Blames the director for a yield drop concentrated in board-approved award tiers; punishes the wrong party and leaves the cause in place.
Addresses the tier pattern that the evidence supports; needs modelling of net revenue and must be decided before award letters.
Low-cost, addresses the RD merit-review bottleneck, but is not the main yield driver.
Only sensible if a lost-document cause is confirmed; not yet established.
Enough to act on the award schedule now; the remaining unknowns (RD turnaround share, documents) do not change that step.

output.brief: The fall in enrolment is mostly a scholarship effect, not an Admissions Office failure. Yield dropped sharply only in the tiers whose merit awards were cut (Dean's and Merit, about 45% to 32%). The Presidential tier, whose award was unchanged, stayed flat, and applications and admits both rose. Early-action admits, who never went through the new portal, also fell by a similar amount, so the portal delay cannot be the main cause. Replacing the Admissions Director would punish the wrong party and leave the cause in place. Next steps: take the award schedule back to the finance committee with a net-revenue model before next cycle's award letters go out. Also set a monthly regular-decision turnaround target, since the merit-review team was cut and decisions took about 38 days. My confidence is moderate. I did not check the staffing records or the document-loss claims, so the portal's share of the problem is still unresolved.
